projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Kathryn Martin was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: This is the beginning of an interview with Kathryn Martin at her home at 100 South Indian Hill in Claremont, California Mrs. Martin is 79 years old, born on January 28th, 1923. My name is Melissa Lam, and I am the interviewer Mrs. Martin, can you state for the record what war and branch of service you served in?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: I served in the U.S. Coast Guard.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: So, why don't we go over just some background information?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Where were you born and raised?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: I was born and raised--you need the city or just a state?

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: City and state.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Okay. I was born in West Southfield, Connecticut.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: What did your parents do?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: My mother stayed home, housewife; my dad was head of Connecticut Valley, which is tobacco, tobacco company, worked in a tobacco company. He was manager of raising the crops and all.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Do you have any brothers and sisters?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Yes, I do.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: How old were you when the war started?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Oh, I was--let's see. It started in, if I can remember correctly, I don't know if it was '40-- '41, I think. Am I correct?

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: It was '41.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: I'd just gotten out of high school.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Do you remember events from when the war started, Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Oh, gosh, it was on a Sunday in December, and, oh, I just happened to flip the radio on and I heard. It was just a shock to all of us. Yes, I remember it very well.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: And so you had just graduated high school?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: What were your plans right after that, before the war?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, I was going to--Dad, of course, wanted us to all go to college. I was going to go into nursing, but then I felt like I--very patriotic, and I felt like I was doing, you know, doing it for my country. And I knew it was important that they did have women there, because actually what we did, we replaced jobs of men going overseas. So we could, you know, do anything, really. It was amazing, the different things we did. Of course, the ones that had a college degree, automatically when they enlisted got to go to officers training, and I was going to do it on a GI bill when I got out. So, I was a little younger than some of them, and that does make a difference; but, I wanted to be a pharmacist then.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Was there a lot of recruiting that went on, recruiting women?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: There wasn't--I don't think everybody was conscious of it, but those that were interested in it would check it out. And what I did, I was going into the Navy. But at that particular time it was quota reject, they wanted you to wait a few months. So, I got impatient, and I got on the train, didn't tell anybody in my family, got on the train and went in to Boston and enlisted in the Coast Guard.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: That must have been quite a shock to your family.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, they know. I always said I was going to get away from tobacco row. But, anyways, I was working at Pratt & Whitney. But I was thinking: Oh, you know, I've just got to go into the military, so I checked it out. But I didn't hear a lot of girls talking about. A lot of them were more interested in defense jobs, I think, money, but I was looking at something else. I wanted to get away from home and see the world.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Was your family supportive of your joining?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, see I never--my dad wasn't very happy, because he'd been in the First World War, he'd been over in France, and he said he saw a lot of the nurses. He just thought maybe it wasn't the way he wanted his daughter to go. But then when I came home from boot camp and was talking about all that I was going to do, he felt a little different, you know.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: So when did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: And you talked about boot camp, what kind of training did you have in boot camp?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, you know, they had just moved the women's training from Miami, Florida up to Brooklyn, New York. And on our base, it was a big base, half of it was men and half of it was women; where down, you know, in Miami it was all women. So it was a bigger set-up. And we, every Saturday had reviews, and we won lots of times for our marching because we had a marine drill sergeant who was tough on us. So I always remember when we won a couple of Saturdays, see, we competed against men. These reviews were rather interesting.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Did you train with men?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: No, we trained separately and had our classes. We had to go to classes, and then we had certain duties, you know, they're very, you know, disciplined, which didn't bother me at all. Some of the girls, you know, didn't like it, but I was brought up in a very strict family so it was easy to be disciplined.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Did you have much interaction with the men?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Yeah, we did. We had dances and our reviews, when we were at liberty, which mostly was the weekends.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: What kind of-- Did they treat you as equals or they tried to take care of you?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, I don't know how they really felt, but there were a lot of young men and they were very happy to escort a SPAR somewhere. Of course, I got to see a lot, Central Park and some of the museums. There was a lot of things we did.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: You mentioned some of the other girls didn't like the discipline?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Yeah, some of them, because, you know, some people maybe had a different background, I don't know. They didn't realize that you had to do what they said. You don't, when you get out on your own or you go to school, you might find that you have a little more say. No. They cut all our hair off. And we had inspections. Every day an officer would come through with her white gloves, and if she found any dust, you can even put it under the spring, and, as they say, you have to drop a dime, it's so tight, everything. All our clothes, we had to roll them up and put them in our drawer.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Did you find that the other women joined for the same reasons you did or were there a lot of different reasons for joining the Coast Guards?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, I think most of them joined were patriotic, I think they felt like I did, that they were doing something for the country. Yeah, I think so.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: After your training, did they send you to different _____?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, here's how they did it. When we finished our classes and graduated, they gave us four choices where we wanted to be stationed. And some of the girls said they stationed rather close to your homes. So what I did, I knew where I wanted to go, I wanted to go to California. So I put for the first choice definitely not the south, which would have been all right, but, you know, I was raised--you know, there's no problem in north and south any more, but they say that they favor their southerners. That's nice. And I put California and didn't give them any other choice. But they could have--I think over the half of the girls put in for California and only six of us were chosen, and I was thrilled. They kept calling off the names where you were going to be stationed, I never dreamed I'd get it. So, I guess I had not given them too much choice.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: When you got to California, did you live on the beach or ______?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, I first was sent--we, of course, went by train, because during the war that's what they did. We all--they'd treat you, you know, we always had first choice. And I went to Long Beach, which was the headquarters. But when I got there, they told me that-- they sent a few of us to San Diego to be stationed. I don't know how they chose, whether it's something to do with your background. So my permanent base was a Coast Guard station in San Diego, which is right across from North Island. And, I have to say, my husband was a pilot, Coast Guard pilot.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: You met your husband when--

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: We were stationed together. He was the cutest man on the base.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: So, did you get to travel much around California?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, what I--I was lucky because I got leave at least three times the first year to go to the East Coast back home. And then I signed up for Hawaii. There was only two places they'd send us, was Alaska and Hawaii. So I thought: Well, I'll get to Hawaii. Well, you know, the war was starting to wind down and there was probably people before me on the list; so, I never did get to go to Hawaii. But they did issue me clothes for Alaska. I have a beautiful coat, wool coat, all lined, that I never wore, military, because I never got to the Alaska.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: What sort of job did you do?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, when I first went in, they needed somebody desperately in the post office on base. So I worked there for a while. And, of course, I got to know everybody on base. And then they needed help in personnel so they put me over there. But my last job was I worked the switchboard for the pilots when they have crashes at sea. The pilots have a ready room and they wait for calls. See, he was in Air/Sea Rescue. At that time they flew planes, now today a lot of it is done by helicopter, as you probably see. So I--and I was there until I got out.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: It must have been a very hard job.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Oh, it was, it was. A lot of the experience, we had parachute riggers, girls, for the pilots; and they had small boats that some of the SPARS operate to take the men out to their planes that are on water. See, they flew planes PBYs and PBMs that landed on the water. They did many things. But a lot of your military, when you go in you have to have KP, I never had any of that. You see, the Coast Guard has a lot fewer women. And I figured, when I went to enlist I figured I would get a better chance in doing something that I wanted to do while I was there, but I never did get to pharmacy school. But later in life, after I had three boys in college, I went into nursing when I was 49.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: So I did get a little bit.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: And how did you feel, being among the first women?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: We were very honored, we're very honored. We've had a lot of honors. Last year they commissioned a new Coast Guard cutter up in Kodiak, Alaska, and it was a three-day reunion for all the ladies that served, the ones like me, first ones to go in. And then in Washington, D.C., you probably have heard about, I think it was in '92 they had a memorial built to all the women in the military, and we got special honors there because we were, you know, the original ones. Well, they called us charter members, actually.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: So when you went into the service, did you see that as being just a war-time thing or did you--

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: I would have loved to have stayed in. But during the war, the Coast Guard is under the Navy; and so when the war was over, they were--they more or less, some of the girls, joined the Navy, which I could have done, but I got married instead. But anyways, yeah, we had to get out, more or less. There's a few that they left in Long Beach in personnel, you know, because they still had a lot of work to do discharging a lot of the women. And the ones that had the most points that had been in the longest had a chance of getting out sooner. So I was not in the beginning.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: So how long did your recruitment last?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Just less than two years.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: What were some of your most memorable experiences?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Oh, let's see. While I was in, well, you know what I did--this is a memorable to me, maybe nobody else--but we had a Navy man that was in charge of post office, so he went on leave, so that means I had to take over and pick up the mail downtown San Diego, and wear a big gun. And they all kidded me, I wasn't very big and I had a big gun. But, see, any time you handle military stuff especially during war. So I knew that in San Diego they had some special places they delivered the mail. So up near Rose Grand, the veterans are very--they had a secret door, this is the truth, and they had a tunnel, and I had to deliver. And I had known some young Coast Guard men who picked me up in a Jeep and helped me get the mail and he escorted me up there. I had to deliver it personally because I was in charge of the post office. So, we went into the store--I never knew about it, I think it's still there--and you go through a tunnel and then you come out right on the waterfront. And there's what they call a shack, radio shack, more or less, and they have Coast Guard at all times there, night and day, because during the war they're always checking for incoming on the coastline. So, to me, that was the most exciting.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Did you know people who were in the Armed Forces abroad?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, I'll tell you, I met a few when I was stationed here in San Diego on our days off from liberty, we called it. The Naval Hospital, there was a lot young men coming from overseas who had been wounded, and I got to meet some, write letters to their family. And I can tell you this, I never saw such a happy bunch of men; parts of their body, limbs gone, but they were thankful to be alive. So we donated time there, so I did meet a few that had seen some rough duty.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: What was your whole perception about the war?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, I felt that we really had no choice, we were attacked at Pearl Harbor and that we just had to make the most of it. And I was always very proud, I never disgraced my uniform. And I'll tell you this, when I was stationed in San Diego, went out on Liberty, we were watched closer than most women, their moms watching them. Because if anybody--there's MPs and SPs, if you got out of line or got drunk or anything, they'd get that wagon and pull you back to base.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: So, did you feel the uniform entitled to you show a certain dignity?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Yes, I did. I did. You know, I just felt, you know, it was an honor to be in the war for your country. I'm very patriotic, very much so. And most of us were, you know, very well behaved. I met some all over the United States, girls from everywhere, some I'm still in contact with. So it was--and, of course, we used to see a lot of men be hauled away, but--and I think we had--we still have a bond, all the women that I meet with, you know, we have a bond. It's just there, you can't explain it.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: You shared a very special time together.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Oh, yes, yes. And some of the women were decorated up in Alaska, because they had crashes up there and a couple of the nurses dove in and saved lives, and I don't think people realize.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Wow, that's a cool story.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Very special, yes.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: They dove in the water and they--

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Yeah, well they have--with the Coast Guard, I don't know just what technique or too much. I think they wore wet suits. And I don't think people realize that. We had some brave women. The nurses, you know, they probably in the field, you know, had injuries. They have certainly dedicated their lives to do that. That's really what I wanted to do.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Did your family ever come out to see you on the base?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: No. No, they never did.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: How did you--did you write letters to them?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Oh, yes. Oh, yes. See, I got to go--I was one of the lucky ones, I got liberty three times.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: So most of your communications was ______?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: But I did meet a Navy man that was engaged to my sister. She didn't see him but his ship docked in San Diego so I got to see him. And that was exciting, you know, to see somebody that's in your family.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Was it hard being away from them for such a long period?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: I was very--no.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Very independent?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Very independent, yes.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: So, when your service ended, you were in your early 20s at the time?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Twenty, 23.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: So it ended in '45?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Yeah. The end of '45, I got out.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: How did you feel once that came to an end?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, I was going to have a new life. I really liked military, some couldn't wait to get out but I loved it. I just thought it was an opportunity to see the country, more of the country. So I was one that probably would have stayed in.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: When were you engaged to your husband?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: The day after I got my discharge, he came down to Long Beach.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Was he stationed at Long Beach as well?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: No. He'd gotten out before me.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: He could have been a career man but he just wanted to have a family. Some men do.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Did he join because--

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Oh, he was in before the war.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Yes. He was already onboard ship. And he took competitive exam against all of the young college kids, he got one of the highest grades, that's how he got in. I was very proud of him. Of course, I didn't know him until he came to San Diego, but he was in Long Beach.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: But he got out before the war ended, he was discharged?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: So, what did you do right after the war ended and you were discharged?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, I did have to go back home. In fact, I got married in my church. My husband was from Victorville, never heard of desert too much coming from the east coast, and that's where I lived when I first got out.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Did you go to school again?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: I would have liked to. No, I didn't. Having my babies slowed me down.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: We talked about that you maintained a lot of friendships?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: How do you keep in contact now? Do you see each other?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: No. We'll see some of them in mid-west; Christmas cards, except for women that I meet here. These ladies are all from Southern California. In fact, our party Saturday's with the Navy. And we had special doings, oh, must have been a few months ago in Long Beach at the Officers' Club: We had Marines, Navy and Coast Guards. And there are a lot of interesting things. We have present day military, girls that are serving aboardship, which we couldn't do in those days, and we hear their experiences and it's really different now. But they don't have the--well, maybe they will before it's all over, the same feel when you're in that it's war-time. Of course, now we don't know, the Coast Guard is playing an important part now.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Do you think had the war not happened that you would have taken that route?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: I would have gone on to school, yeah, I would have. And I had a job with an insurance company, I quit that; and then I went to Pratt & Whitney and I started a office job. And if you were a--I was afraid they wouldn't release me, but then I wasn't making--working on planes or anything, and that's what it was, factory; so, I very quietly left and didn't tell them where I'm going. That's me.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: So, you went back home and got married and had your children. You stayed at (inaudible)?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Yes. I stayed there until I was 49.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: And you were still living back at home?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Not back east, I've always lived out here in California, ever since I got married I lived out here. I went to work--went into nursing, I was 49. See, I did get it. But then we had the third boy starting college and my daughter would be going, so I went to work. My husband said: "Why do you want to just get yourself an easier job?" I said, "If I'm going to work, I'm going to do something I always wanted to do." So, I feel very good about that.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: How do you feel about nursing? Was that very rewarding?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Oh, very much so. In fact, I wasn't a RN, but the nurses all wanted me to go on, but my husband doesn't like me working some weekends. Oh, yes, it was very--I've just--some of them have the feel for nursing, compassion, you got to have some. And some, you know, not too happy that all is to do. But I was a very happy person when I was in nursing.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Do you think you would have wanted to serve as a nurse?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Yes, I would have. I would have, yes, I would have.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: How would you say that your service and your experience with the Coast Guard affected your life? Has it changed your life?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Oh, it has, it has. I think when you travel around, you meet all kinds of people, all situations, it broadens your outlook on life. I can't believe, you know, I was brought up when I was a kid sort of out in the country. Oh, yes, it was--oh, I'd go in now if I was younger. I would go in again.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: You would do it again?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Yes, I would.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Is there anything else that you'd like to talk about?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Of course. I have a few regrets that I didn't go in sooner so I could have gotten the school I wanted. I really wanted to be a pharmacist and then go on, you know.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: If you had joined earlier, you would have been able to do that?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: I think I would have, yes.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: What were you doing in the beginning of the war?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: After boot camp I came out here. Now, women did--one of my very best friends, she was an intelligence officer, she lives over in Bradbury, and she did all the coding, a lot of the coding for the military. It's amazing, some of the jobs. But she was a little older and she had a college degree, that did help you. They had a wonderful school, Hunter College in New York is where they trained all their officers.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Were a lot of your officers women or did you have men as officers as well?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, let's see, of course, we had a CO on base and, of course, we have to respect him; but I had women officers, basically. And we didn't live on base in San Diego but we had quarters. There were a few of the girls had to work switchboards at night, so they had living quarters there. But what we did, we had a hotel downtown San Diego; instead of having barracks, we lived in a hotel. And we had a lot of activity. Like Saturday some of the Navy were invited, Marines; in fact, I met a Marine too, of course, San Diego is full of Marines. But I ended up with my husband. But we had our fun times, but we had a lot of restrictions. And I ate on base. I ate on base, our mess hall was on base.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: So you didn't actually live right on the base?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: No. They would pick up--we'd have several vans going in the morning from the hotel to the base, and we called it an air station because it was pilots, and we would do our duty on base; and, if we had night duty, you could stay there, and some of the girls did. Then we were brought back to our hotel. We ate there though, we didn't have any food in our hotel.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: How many girls did you live with in a room?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Let's see, in boot camp, we had four bunks in boot camp. Then we--then at the hotel, we had rooms. And I did have a roommate, there were two of us.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: So you would get up in the morning, go to work, come back, would you have just that night to yourself or would you--

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Sometimes we had duty at the hotel and sometimes we had liberty. They had a system, we weren't allowed to go out every night, you know, we were restricted, except on our time.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: What kind of duties did you have to do?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Check-in, we have to know everybody who's staying there, we have to know who's coming in, we have to put the time down. We had a time limit. I mean, we were pretty well--and if we were sick, you know, we could go over to--well, on base they did have an infirmary for women and men, we could be checked out there. Then they'd say, "You can go back and sleep in your room today."

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Did a lot of the other girls end up meeting future husbands?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Oh, you'd be amazed, yes, although about half of the men were married on base. See, I knew everybody was married because I'd see them pick up their mail. Yes, it's true, they did.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: How was the dating while you were serving there?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: There was a lot of availability.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: They didn't have any, like, guidelines of what you were--

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, no, no. We were restricted to go to Old Mexico, but if you got permission. So I did get to go over the border, but then we had a curfew time we had to leave. I went with several pairs. So, being new out in California, I did want to go there. But everything we did, we more or less have to have a slip, you know. They keep track of you, very much so.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Even when you were going on leave, did you have to let them know where you were going to be?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Yes. In case they might want to call you, something came up, they need you to come there immediately. Some did too, went on leave and they were called back for certain jobs if they needed them. And then one Easter, which was really fun, there was a group of us, we didn't really have liberty that day so they arranged, one of the Coast Guards' smaller boats, said they would take the SPARS that kind of had the duty, would take them over to Catalina for the day. So that was all restricted during the war. So we got to go over there and swim and eat, so that was sort of a treat for us. I had some pictures when we were sailing over there. I ought to show you a picture of me in uniform.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: I thought you might want to see it. First pictures, I don't have all of them. There was a photographer on base that was taking a lot of pictures of me in an airplane, you know, they have a photographer there. They put out a weekly--a month, month, once a month, whatever goes on on the base with the pilots, where they went, where they rescued. I just thought you might want to see what my uniform looks like. That's small. They made a movie on us. See if you can pick me out, I'm in the front row.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: That's me. Here we got out our uniform. This is one day we were sailing on the ship there.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Did you like your uniform? It looks nice.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Yeah, I did. I have all my uniforms and all my husband's; I've got all his gold wings too. Here's one picture of me, see how funny we were? I was climbing up in a plane. This is me looking up. Yeah, there's one photographer who always wanted to photograph me. So, that's how our uniforms looked.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: It's very nice.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: See, the Navy girls have same Navy blue but they have an anchor, we have a shield. I don't have my coat here. I was going to show you my--see, I have all my uniforms. And you have summer uniforms where you can--we had some seersucker ones, and we had two kinds of hat. This is--I think they call that a campaign hat, and then one with the broom. See I have all--but the museums have been asking for women in the Coast Guard, they want them in the museum, but I have a granddaughter who's 16 up in Seattle and she's very conscientious, so I'm leaving her my uniforms.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Did you tell your kids about your experience?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Oh, I tell my grandchildren war stories. They're in college, they think it's really something; because I was always a live wire, I didn't miss much. See that picture that you see there, that was taken in front of a fair in San Diego. They made a movie on the SPARs and they wanted us to come off the base and take our pictures.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Oh they made a movie back then?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Back then, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Oh, that's very interesting.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Well, see, I think why we--of course, maybe the Navy girls have, I haven't heard. But we were the first women. There's no reason they shouldn't have women in the Coast Guard. And that's what Dorothy Stratton said, she was an officer in the Navy. She got out and said, "I'm going to form-- " We just think the world of her.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: After the SPARS was disbanded, were there still women in the Coast Guard?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: A few, they kept, headquarters in Long Beach, did. But some of the girls went in the Navy, which we had a choice if we wanted to.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Of course, today they're taking women in.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: They're in. I was amazed. We had a speaker not too long ago, a young girl that came off of--a lot of them are getting--becoming officers, they're doing all right, and she spoke of her duty onboardship. I haven't--you know, I'm from the old school, I'm not sure that I think it's best way to go, but women have rights too. I just kind of think, you know, it's not as good, mixing the men and the women. And they told--she told us this, five or six girls that left that were pregnant, so you never know. So, that's how I feel about it, but I think they can do the duty. Now, when we were--when I was in boot camp, they told us we had the same training as the men except with the guns, we were exposed to them, and rowing, they had rowing, water. See, because, you know, Coast Guard, you think of being around the water, so we didn't have rowing, and we didn't have--we were exposed to guns but we didn't train with guns.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: You had the same training as the men?

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: That's what they told us, our schooling. The only time we saw them during the week is when we had our Saturday. And they're beautiful, because you dress up in your dress outfit, and it was really good. So you really concentrate because you want to beat those young ones. But I know we won a couple of them. See, they have some of that. If somebody got out of step, I suppose they would see it. And one thing about what's different about the military is we mustered to everything. We get our orders in the morning. We have revelry, when that goes, you better get up and get dressed. And we marched to everything. We had to form lines to go to our classes, everything. See, it's more military, which I like. I really liked it. It's good training for you.

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Okay. Well, --

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: Do you think you got enough?

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: I do, I have more than enough.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: You can see, I'm still--

sp.speaker: Melissa Lam
sp.p: Thank you, very much.

sp.speaker: Kathryn Martin
sp.p: You're welcome.
